statement:
The Bank of Oslo issues coins made out of two types of metal: aluminium (denoted $A$) and copper (denoted $C$). Morgane has $n$ aluminium coins, and $n$ copper coins, and arranges her $2n$ coins in a row in some arbitrary initial order. Given a fixed positive integer $k \leqslant 2n$, she repeatedly performs the following operation: identify the largest subsequence containing the $k$-th coin from the left which consists of consecutive coins made of the same metal, and move all coins in that subsequence to the left end of the row. For example, if $n=4$ and $k=4$, the process starting from the configuration $A A C C C A C A$ would be
$$
A A C C C A C A \rightarrow C C C A A A C A \rightarrow A A A C C C C A \rightarrow C C C C A A A A \rightarrow \cdots .
$$
Find all pairs $(n, k)$ with $1 \leqslant k \leqslant 2n$ such that for every initial configuration, at some point of the process there will be at most one aluminium coin adjacent to a copper coin.
solution:
Define a block to be a maximal subsequence of consecutive coins made out of the same metal, and let $M^{b}$ denote a block of $b$ coins of metal $M$. The property that there is at most one aluminium coin adjacent to a copper coin is clearly equivalent to the configuration having two blocks, one consisting of all $A$-s and one consisting of all $C$-s.

First, notice that if $k < n$, the sequence $A^{n-1} C^{n-1} A C$ remains fixed under the operation, and will therefore always have 4 blocks. Next, if $k > \frac{3n+1}{2}$, let $a = k - n - 1$, $b = 2n - k + 1$. Then $k > 2a + b$, $k > 2b + a$, so the configuration $A^{a} C^{b} A^{b} C^{a}$ will always have four blocks:
$$
A^{a} C^{b} A^{b} C^{a} \rightarrow C^{a} A^{a} C^{b} A^{b} \rightarrow A^{b} C^{a} A^{a} C^{b} \rightarrow C^{b} A^{b} C^{a} A^{a} \rightarrow A^{a} C^{b} A^{b} C^{a} \rightarrow \ldots
$$
Therefore a pair $(n, k)$ can have the desired property only if $n \leqslant k \leqslant \frac{3n+1}{2}$. We claim that all such pairs in fact do have the desired property. Clearly, the number of blocks in a configuration cannot increase, so whenever the operation is applied, it either decreases or remains constant. We show that unless there are only two blocks, after a finite amount of steps the number of blocks will decrease.

Consider an arbitrary configuration with $c \geqslant 3$ blocks. We note that as $k \geqslant n$, the leftmost block cannot be moved, because in this case all $n$ coins of one type are in the leftmost block, meaning there are only two blocks. If a block which is not the leftmost or rightmost block is moved, its neighbor blocks will be merged, causing the number of blocks to decrease.

Hence the only case in which the number of blocks does not decrease in the next step is if the rightmost block is moved. If $c$ is odd, the leftmost and the rightmost blocks are made of the same metal, so this would merge two blocks. Hence $c \geqslant 4$ must be even. Suppose there is a configuration of $c$ blocks with the $i$-th block having size $a_{i}$ so that the operation always moves the rightmost block:
$$
A^{a_{1}} \ldots A^{a_{c-1}} C^{a_{c}} \rightarrow C^{a_{c}} A^{a_{1}} \ldots A^{a_{c-1}} \rightarrow A^{a_{c-1}} C^{a_{c}} A^{a_{1}} \ldots C^{a_{c-2}} \rightarrow \ldots
$$
Because the rightmost block is always moved, $k \geqslant 2n+1-a_{i}$ for all $i$. Because $\sum a_{i} = 2n$, summing this over all $i$ we get $c k \geqslant 2c n + c - \sum a_{i} = 2c n + c - 2n$, so $k \geqslant 2n + 1 - \frac{2n}{c} \geqslant \frac{3n}{2} + 1$. But this contradicts $k \leqslant \frac{3n+1}{2}$. Hence at some point the operation will not move the rightmost block, meaning that the number of blocks will decrease, as desired.
ratingReason: Track the number of monochromatic blocks, isolate the cyclic last-block obstruction, and construct counterexamples on both sides of the permitted interval.

statement:
Let $\mathbb{R}_{>0}$ be the set of positive real numbers. Find all functions $f: \mathbb{R}_{>0} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}_{>0}$ such that, for every $x \in \mathbb{R}_{>0}$, there exists a unique $y \in \mathbb{R}_{>0}$ satisfying
$$
x f(y)+y f(x) \leqslant 2 .
$$
solution:
The unique solution is $f(x)=1/x$. This works because $x/y+y/x\geq2$, with equality only when $y=x$.

Call $(x,y)$ admissible when $xf(y)+yf(x)\leq2$. Suppose an admissible pair has $x\ne y$. By uniqueness, neither $(x,x)$ nor $(y,y)$ is admissible, so $xf(x)>1$ and $yf(y)>1$. But AM-GM gives
$$xf(y)+yf(x)\geq2\sqrt{xf(x)\,yf(y)}>2,$$
a contradiction. Thus the admissible partner of every $x$ is $x$ itself, and $f(x)\leq1/x$ for all $x>0$.

If $f(x)<1/x$ for some $x$, choose $a$ with $x<a<1/f(x)$. Then
$$af(x)+xf(a)\leq af(x)+x/a<1+1=2.$$
This makes $(x,a)$ admissible with $a\ne x$, another contradiction. Hence $f(x)=1/x$ everywhere.
ratingReason: Uniqueness first excludes unequal admissible pairs by AM-GM; a nearby input then rules out strict inequality in the bound f(x)≤1/x.

statement: Fix a positive integer $k$ and a finite set $S$ of odd primes. Show that, up to rotation and reflection, at most one circular ordering of $S$ has this property: the product of each pair of adjacent primes equals $x^2+x+k$ for some positive integer $x$.
solution: Allow $x=0$ as well. If $p<r$ and $pr=x^2+x+k$, then $0\leq x<r$. A quadratic congruence modulo the prime $r$ has at most two roots, so $r$ has at most two smaller possible neighbours. If these are $p<q<r$, write $pr=x^2+x+k$ and $qr=y^2+y+k$ with $x<y<r$. Vieta gives $x+y=r-1$, and subtraction gives $y-x=q-p$. Substitution yields $4pq=(r-p-q)^2+4k-1$. Since $r-p-q$ is odd, putting $z=(|r-p-q|-1)/2$ gives $pq=z^2+z+k$. Thus the two neighbours are themselves compatible. Induct on $|S|$: remove its largest prime from any valid circle. Its two neighbours are forced and the resulting smaller circle is valid, so induction determines the circle uniquely.
ratingReason: The unusual interaction between a quadratic congruence and cycle uniqueness requires discovering a closure lemma for the two smaller prime neighbours, then inducting after deleting the largest prime.

statement:
Let $ABCD E$ be a convex pentagon such that $BC = DE$. Assume there is a point $T$ inside $ABCDE$ with $TB = TD$, $TC = TE$ and $\angle TBA = \angle AET$. Let lines $CD$ and $CT$ intersect line $AB$ at points $P$ and $Q$, respectively, and let lines $CD$ and $DT$ intersect line $AE$ at points $R$ and $S$, respectively. Assume that points $P, B, A, Q$ and $R, E, A, S$ respectively, are collinear and occur on their lines in this order. Prove that the points $P, S, Q, R$ are concyclic.

(Slovakia)
solution:
By the conditions we have $BC = DE$, $CT = ET$ and $TB = TD$, so the triangles $TBC$ and $TDE$ are congruent, in particular $\angle BTC = \angle DTE$.

In triangles $TBQ$ and $TES$ we have $\angle TBQ = \angle SET$ and $\angle QTB = 180^\circ - \angle BTC = 180^\circ - \angle DTE = \angle ETS$, so these triangles are similar to each other. It follows that $\angle TSE = \angle BQT$ and
$$
\frac{TD}{TQ} = \frac{TB}{TQ} = \frac{TE}{TS} = \frac{TC}{TS}.
$$
By rearranging this relation we get $TD \cdot TS = TC \cdot TQ$, so $C, D, Q$ and $S$ are concyclic. (Alternatively, we can get $\angle CQD = \angle CSD$ from the similar triangles $TCS$ and $TDQ$.) Hence, $\angle DCQ = \angle DSQ$.

Finally, from the angles of triangle $CQP$ we get
$$
\angle RPQ = \angle RCQ - \angle PQC = \angle DSQ - \angle DSR = \angle RSQ,
$$
which proves that $P, Q, R$ and $S$ are concyclic.
ratingReason: SSS congruence creates a second triangle similarity, whose length relation gives the auxiliary cyclic quadrilateral needed for the final angle chase.

statement:
Find all triples of positive integers $(a, b, p)$ with $p$ prime and
$$
a^{p} = b! + p.
$$
solution:
The solutions are $(a,b,p)=(2,2,2)$ and $(3,4,3)$.

Clearly $a>1$. If $a<p$ and $a\leq b$, then $a$ divides $b!$ and $a^p$, so $a\mid p$, impossible. If instead $b<a<p$, then $b!\leq a!<a^p-p$, also impossible. For the last inequality, $p\geq3$ and $a!\leq a^{p-1}$ give $a^p-a!\geq(a-1)a^{p-1}\geq2^{p-1}>p$.

Suppose $a>p$. Then $b!=a^p-p>p!$, so $b>p$ and $p\mid a$. The valuation of $a^p-p$ at $p$ is exactly one, hence $b<2p$. If $p<a<p^2$, the integer $a/p$ is between two and $p-1$, so it divides both $b!$ and $a^p$ and consequently divides $p$, a contradiction. If $a\geq p^2$, then
$$a^p\geq p^{2p}>(2p-1)!+p\geq b!+p.$$
Here $(2p-1)!\leq p^{2p-1}$ follows by pairing $j$ with $2p-j$ for $1\leq j<p$. This again contradicts the equation.

Thus $a=p$. The primes two and three give precisely the two listed solutions. For $p\geq5$, we have $b! =p^p-p>p!$, so $b\geq p+1$. The distinct integers $2$ and $(p+1)/2$ occur in $p!$, showing $p+1\mid p!$ and therefore $(p+1)^2\mid b!$. On the other hand, binomial expansion at $p=(p+1)-1$ gives
$$p^p-p\equiv p(p+1)-1-p=p^2-1\not\equiv0\pmod{(p+1)^2}.$$
This final contradiction excludes all larger primes.

statement:
Alice fills the fields of an $n \times n$ board with numbers from $1$ to $n^{2}$, each number being used exactly once. She then counts the total number of good paths on the board. A good path is a sequence of fields of arbitrary length (including $1$) such that:
(i) The first field in the sequence is one that is only adjacent to fields with larger numbers,
(ii) Each subsequent field in the sequence is adjacent to the previous field,
(iii) The numbers written on the fields in the sequence are in increasing order.

Two fields are considered adjacent if they share a common side. Find the smallest possible number of good paths Alice can obtain, as a function of $n$.
solution:
We will call any field that is only adjacent to fields with larger numbers a well. Other fields will be called non-wells. Let us make a second $n \times n$ board $B$ where in each field we will write the number of good sequences which end on the corresponding field in the original board $A$. We will thus look for the minimal possible value of the sum of all entries in $B$.

We note that any well has just one good path ending in it, consisting of just the well, and that any other field has the number of good paths ending in it equal to the sum of this quantity for all the adjacent fields with smaller values, since a good path can only come into the field from a field of lower value. Therefore, if we fill in the fields in $B$ in increasing order with respect to their values in $A$, it follows that each field not adjacent to any already filled field will receive a $1$, while each field adjacent to already filled fields will receive the sum of the numbers already written on these adjacent fields.

We note that there is at least one well in $A$, that corresponding with the field with the entry $1$ in $A$. Hence, the sum of values of fields in $B$ corresponding to wells in $A$ is at least $1$. We will now try to minimize the sum of the non-well entries, i.e. of the entries in $B$ corresponding to the non-wells in $A$. We note that we can ascribe to each pair of adjacent fields the value of the lower assigned number and that the sum of non-well entries will then equal to the sum of the ascribed numbers. Since the lower number is still at least $1$, the sum of non-well entries will at least equal the number of pairs of adjacent fields, which is $2 n(n-1)$. Hence, the total minimum sum of entries in $B$ is at least $2 n^{2}-2 n+1$. The necessary conditions for the minimum to be achieved is for there to be only one well and for no two entries in $B$ larger than $1$ to be adjacent to each other.

We will now prove that the lower limit of $2 n^{2}-2 n+1$ entries can be achieved. This amounts to finding a way of marking a certain set of squares, those that have a value of $1$ in $B$, such that no two unmarked squares are adjacent and that the marked squares form a connected tree with respect to adjacency.

For $n=1$ and $n=2$ the markings are respectively the lone field and the L-trimino. Now, for $n>2$, let $s=2$ for $n \equiv 0,2 \bmod 3$ and $s=1$ for $n \equiv 1 \bmod 3$. We will take indices $k$ and $l$ to be arbitrary non-negative integers. For $n \geqslant 3$ we will construct a path of marked squares in the first two columns consisting of all squares of the form $(1, i)$ where $i$ is not of the form $6k+s$ and $(2, j)$ where $j$ is of the form $6k+s-1, 6k+s$ or $6+s+1$. Obviously, this path is connected. Now, let us consider the fields $(2, 6k+s)$ and $(1, 6k+s+3)$. For each considered field $(i, j)$ we will mark all squares of the form $(l, j)$ for $l>i$ and $(i+2k, j \pm 1)$. One can easily see that no set of marked fields will produce a cycle, that the only fields of the unmarked form $(1, 6k+s), (2+2l+1, 6k+s \pm 1)$ and $(2+2l, 6k+s+3 \pm 1)$ and that no two are adjacent, since the consecutive considered fields are in columns of opposite parity. Examples of markings are given for $n=3,4,5,6,7$, and the corresponding constructions for $A$ and $B$ are given for $n=5$.

statement: Partition $\{1,\ldots,1989\}$ into 117 disjoint sets of seventeen elements, all having the same sum.
solution:
For $1\le i\le117$, define a triple beginning with $i$. If $i\le59$, complete it with $i+175$ and $353-2i$. If $i\ge60$, complete it with $i+58$ and $470-2i$.

Every triple sums to 528. Their first entries cover 1 through 117. Their second entries cover 176 through 234 in the first case and 118 through 175 in the second. Their third entries cover the odd integers 235 through 351 and the even integers 236 through 350. Hence the triples partition 1 through 351.

Pair the remaining integers 352 through 1989 by pairing $j$ with $2341-j$. There are 819 disjoint pairs, each of sum 2341. Give any seven pairs to each of the 117 triples, using every pair once. Every resulting set has $3+14=17$ elements and sum $528+7\cdot2341=16915$, as required.
ratingReason: Build a balanced partition of the first 351 integers into triples using two complementary parity ranges, then distribute equal-sum pairs to reach seventeen elements per group.

statement: In acute triangle $ABC$, the internal angle bisectors meet its circumcircle again at $A_1,B_1,C_1$. Let $A_0,B_0,C_0$ be the corresponding excenters. Prove $[A_0B_0C_0]=2[AC_1BA_1CB_1]\ge4[ABC]$.
solution:
Let $I$ be the incenter. The arc-midpoint lemma gives $A_1B=A_1C=A_1I=A_1A_0$; in particular $A_1$ is the midpoint of $IA_0$. One proof uses $\angle IBA_0=\angle ICA_0=90^\circ$, placing $B,C$ on the circle with diameter $IA_0$, whose centre lies on $AA_0$ and on the perpendicular bisector of $BC$, hence at $A_1$ when the two lines are distinct. In the isosceles case the same midpoint identity follows by continuity from non-isosceles triangles.

Therefore $[IBA_0C]=2[IBA_1C]$, and the two cyclic versions also hold. Summing these three area decompositions of the excentral triangle and the hexagon proves the identity.

Let $H$ be the orthocenter, which lies inside $ABC$. Its reflection across $BC$ lies on the circumcircle on the arc $BC$ away from $A$. The arc midpoint $A_1$ maximises the perpendicular distance to $BC$ on that arc. Hence $[BCH]\le[BCA_1]$. Summing the three versions gives
$$[ABC]\le[BCA_1]+[CAB_1]+[ABC_1].$$
The hexagon is the original triangle plus these three exterior caps, so its area is at least $2[ABC]$. The claimed second inequality follows from the identity.
ratingReason: Arc midpoints bisect the incenter–excenter segments, giving the exact area identity; reflected orthocenters and maximal chord heights then establish the area inequality.

statement: A set $S$ of $n$ plane points has no three collinear. From every point, at least $k$ other points are at one common distance. Prove $k<1/2+\sqrt{2n}$.
solution:
Count pairs $(P,\{A,B\})$ of distinct points of $S$ with $PA=PB$. For each apex $P$, the hypothesis supplies at least $\binom k2$ such unordered bases, so the count is at least $n\binom k2$.

For each base $\{A,B\}$, possible apexes lie on its perpendicular bisector. At most two points of $S$ lie on that line, since no three are collinear. Thus the count is at most $2\binom n2=n(n-1)$.

Consequently $k(k-1)\le2(n-1)$, or $(k-1/2)^2\le2n-7/4<2n$. Since $k\ge1$, taking square roots proves $k<1/2+\sqrt{2n}$.
ratingReason: Count isosceles triples by their apex and by their base; no three collinear points limits each perpendicular bisector to two possible apexes.

statement: Let $ABCD$ be a convex quadrilateral with $AB=AD+BC$. An interior point $P$ has distance $h$ from the line $CD$ and satisfies $AP=AD+h$ and $BP=BC+h$. Prove $1/\sqrt h\ge1/\sqrt{AD}+1/\sqrt{BC}$.
solution:
Write $a=AD$ and $b=BC$. The disks centred at $A$ and $B$ with radii $a,b$ are externally tangent, since $AB=a+b$. The disk centred at $P$ with radius $h$ is externally tangent to both and tangent to the line $CD$.

The open disk at $P$ meets none of the quadrilateral's sides: $AD$ and $BC$ lie in the first two disks, $AB$ is covered by those disks, and $CD$ lies on a tangent line. Because $P$ is inside the quadrilateral, its entire disk is contained in the quadrilateral. All four vertices belong to the convex hull of the first two disks, so the disk at $P$ is contained in that hull as well.

On the side of $AB$ containing $P$, the part of this hull outside the first two disks is the bounded gap between their arcs and their common external tangent $t$. Among disks in this gap tangent to both original disks, choose one of maximum radius $r$. Such a maximum exists by compactness. It must also touch $t$: otherwise increase $r$ slightly and move its centre along the continuous intersection of the circles of radii $a+r,b+r$ about $A,B$, on the same side of $AB$. The strict clearance from $t$ persists, contradicting maximality. The two centres exist continuously for every positive radius because the triangle inequalities are strict.

Let $D_0,C_0$ be the contact points of the original disks with $t$, and let $E$ be the contact point of the maximum disk. The confinement places $E$ between $D_0,C_0$. Applying Pythagoras to each pair of centres gives
$$D_0C_0=2\sqrt{ab},\qquad D_0E=2\sqrt{ar},\qquad EC_0=2\sqrt{br}.$$
Thus $\sqrt{ab}=\sqrt r(\sqrt a+\sqrt b)$, so $r=ab/(\sqrt a+\sqrt b)^2$. Since $h\le r$, taking reciprocal square roots proves the claimed inequality.
ratingReason: Interpret the distance conditions as three externally tangent disks, prove the small disk is confined by the quadrilateral, and maximise its radius inside the gap between two disks and their common tangent.

statement: For each positive integer $n$, prove there are $n$ consecutive positive integers none of which is a positive integral power of a prime.
solution:
Set $L=(n+1)!$ and take $L^2+2,L^2+3,\ldots,L^2+n+1$. For each $2\le r\le n+1$, write $L=rs$. Then
$$L^2+r=r(rs^2+1).$$
Both factors exceed one, and $\gcd(r,rs^2+1)=1$. Therefore the product has at least two distinct prime divisors and cannot be a prime power. The displayed list has exactly $n$ consecutive positive terms, proving the claim.
ratingReason: A squared factorial makes every term split into two coprime nontrivial factors, which rules out prime powers as well as primes.

statement: Among permutations $(x_1,\ldots,x_{2n})$ of $\{1,\ldots,2n\}$, prove more have an adjacent pair with $|x_i-x_{i+1}|=n$ than have none.
solution:
Let $E_j$ be the event that $j$ and $j+n$ are adjacent. Treating the pair as a block in either order gives $|E_j|=2(2n-1)!$. For $j\ne k$, treating both pairs as blocks gives $|E_j\cap E_k|=4(2n-2)!$.

The two-term inclusion–exclusion bound gives
$$\left|\bigcup_{j=1}^nE_j\right|\ge2n(2n-1)!-4\binom n2(2n-2)!=2n^2(2n-2)!.$$
This exceeds half of $(2n)!$, because
$$2n^2-n(2n-1)=n>0.$$
Thus the required property holds for a strict majority. The lower bound itself follows pointwise: an object belonging to $r$ events contributes $r-\binom r2\le1$ when $r\ge1$, and zero when $r=0$.
ratingReason: Use the first two inclusion–exclusion terms for adjacent complementary pairs; block counting gives an explicit lower bound already exceeding half of all permutations.

statement: Concentric circles have radii $R>r$, and $P$ is fixed on the smaller. A variable line through $P$ cuts the larger circle at $B,C$; its perpendicular through $P$ meets the smaller circle again at $A$, allowing $A=P$ in the tangent case. Find the values of $AB^2+BC^2+CA^2$ and the locus of the midpoint of $BC$.
solution:
Let $M$ be the midpoint of $BC$. Use coordinates $M=(0,0)$, $P=(p,0)$, $O=(0,h)$, $B=(t,0)$, $C=(-t,0)$. Then $p^2+h^2=r^2$, $t^2+h^2=R^2$, and the second smaller-circle intersection is $A=(p,2h)$, including $h=0$.

Therefore
$$AB^2+AC^2+BC^2=(p-t)^2+4h^2+(p+t)^2+4h^2+4t^2=6R^2+2r^2.$$
The set of values is this singleton.

Since $OM\perp PM$, the midpoint $M$ lies on the circle with diameter $OP$. Conversely every point of that circle is the perpendicular projection of $O$ onto a line through $P$ and hence is a corresponding chord midpoint. The endpoint $P$ arises from the line through $P$ perpendicular to $OP$, and $O$ from line $OP$. Thus the entire circle is attained.
ratingReason: Coordinates at the chord midpoint make the moving point’s second intersection explicit and the squared-distance sum cancel; orthogonal projection identifies the full midpoint locus.

statement: Subsets $A_1,\ldots,A_{2n+1}$ of $B$ each contain $2n$ elements, every pair intersects in exactly one element, and every element of $B$ lies in at least two subsets. For which $n$ can the elements be labelled zero or one with exactly $n$ zeros in each $A_i$?
solution:
Fix $A_i$. Its $2n$ elements must each belong to another subset, while the $2n$ other subsets each intersect it only once. Thus every element belongs to exactly two subsets, and there is one element for every pair $\{i,j\}$. Regard that element as an edge of the complete graph on $2n+1$ vertices.

Zero-labelled edges would form a graph of degree $n$ at every vertex. Its degree sum $n(2n+1)$ must be even, forcing $n$ even.

Conversely suppose $n$ is even. Number the vertices modulo $2n+1$ and label an edge zero precisely when its cyclic difference is one of $\pm1,\ldots,\pm n/2$. Each vertex then meets exactly $n$ zero edges; label the rest one. Therefore precisely the positive even integers $n$ work.
ratingReason: The intersection assumptions force the elements to correspond exactly to edges of a complete graph; the handshake parity obstruction and a cyclic regular subgraph give necessity and sufficiency.

statement: Define $f(1)=1$, $f(3)=3$, $f(2n)=f(n)$, $f(4n+1)=2f(2n+1)-f(n)$, and $f(4n+3)=3f(2n+1)-2f(n)$ for positive integers $n$. How many $n\le1988$ satisfy $f(n)=n$?
solution:
Let $R(n)$ be the integer obtained by reversing the binary digits of $n$, discarding leading zeros. Then $R(2n)=R(n)$. If $n$ has $\ell$ binary digits, $R(2n+1)=2^\ell+R(n)$. Consequently
$$R(4n+1)=2^{\ell+1}+R(n)=2R(2n+1)-R(n),$$
$$R(4n+3)=2^{\ell+1}+R(2n+1)=3R(2n+1)-2R(n).$$
Together with $R(1)=1,R(3)=3$, these prove by induction that $f=R$.

The fixed points are therefore exactly the binary palindromes. With $L$ digits their count is $2^{\lceil L/2\rceil-1}$: the first digit is one and the remaining first-half digits determine the rest. For lengths 1 through 10 the counts sum to $1+1+2+2+4+4+8+8+16+16=62$. There are 32 eleven-digit palindromes up to 2047, and exactly two exceed 1988: $2015=(11111011111)_2$ and $2047=(11111111111)_2$. Hence the answer is $62+30=92$.
ratingReason: Recognise and prove binary digit reversal from the recursive formulas, then count binary palindromes with a careful cutoff at 1988.

statement: Prove that the real solution set of $\sum_{k=1}^{70}k/(x-k)\ge5/4$ is a union of disjoint intervals whose total length is 1988.
solution:
Let $F(x)=\sum_{k=1}^{70}k/(x-k)$. On each interval between consecutive poles it is strictly decreasing, with limits $+\infty$ and $-\infty$. On $(70,\infty)$ it decreases from $+\infty$ to zero, and for $x<1$ it is negative. Thus $F(x)=5/4$ has one root $r_k\in(k,k+1)$ for $k<70$ and one $r_{70}>70$. The solution intervals are $(k,r_k]$.

Put $P(x)=\prod_{j=1}^{70}(x-j)$ and $S=1+\cdots+70=2485$. Their endpoints are all 70 roots of
$$Q(x)=\tfrac54P(x)-\sum_{k=1}^{70}k\frac{P(x)}{x-k}.$$
The leading coefficients of $Q$ are $5/4$ and $-(5/4)S-S=-(9/4)S$. Vieta gives $\sum r_k=9S/5$. Therefore the total interval length is $\sum(r_k-k)=4S/5=1988$.
ratingReason: Monotonicity locates one endpoint in each pole interval; clearing denominators and applying Vieta determines the sum of all interval lengths without solving for the endpoints.

statement: In a triangle $ABC$ right-angled at $A$, let $D$ be the altitude foot on $BC$. The line joining the incenters of $ABD$ and $ACD$ meets $AB,AC$ at $K,L$. Prove $[ABC]\ge2[AKL]$.
solution:
Take $A=(0,0)$, $B=(c,0)$, $C=(0,b)$, and write $s=\sqrt{b^2+c^2}$, $h=bc/s=AD$. Then
$$D=(b^2c/s^2,bc^2/s^2),\qquad BD=c^2/s.$$
The incenter $J$ of $ABD$ is the side-length-weighted average
$$J=\frac{hB+cD}{h+c+c^2/s}.$$
Adding its coordinates and simplifying gives $J_x+J_y=h$. Interchanging $b,c$ shows the incenter of $ACD$ also lies on $x+y=h$. Hence their joining line meets the axes at $K=(h,0)$ and $L=(0,h)$.

Thus $[AKL]=h^2/2$ and $[ABC]=bc/2$. The claim is equivalent to
$$bc\ge2h^2=\frac{2b^2c^2}{b^2+c^2},$$
which follows from $b^2+c^2\ge2bc$. Equality holds exactly for $b=c$.
ratingReason: The incenter coordinate formulas reveal that their joining line cuts equal lengths on the two legs, both equal to the altitude; the area bound then reduces to a²+b²≥2ab.

statement: If positive integers $a,b$ satisfy $ab+1\mid a^2+b^2$, prove that $(a^2+b^2)/(ab+1)$ is a square.
solution:
Set $k=(a^2+b^2)/(ab+1)$. Among positive solutions $A^2+B^2=k(AB+1)$ choose one with the smaller coordinate minimal, and label it $B\le A$.

As a quadratic in $A$, its other root is the integer $C=kB-A$, with $AC=B^2-k$. Hence $C<B$. Also
$$(A+1)(C+1)=AC+A+C+1=B^2+(B-1)k+1>0.$$
Since $A+1>0$, we obtain $C>-1$, so the integer $C\ge0$.

If $C>0$, the pair $(C,B)$ is another positive solution for the same $k$ with a smaller minimum coordinate, a contradiction. Therefore $C=0$, and $AC=B^2-k$ gives $k=B^2$. Thus the original quotient is a perfect square.
ratingReason: A minimal-solution Vieta jump must preserve integrality and establish a nonnegative second root; the decisive shifted-product positivity argument makes the descent work but requires substantial discovery.

statement: Let $p_n(k)$ count permutations of $\{1,\ldots,n\}$ with exactly $k$ fixed points. Prove $\sum_{k=0}^n k\,p_n(k)=n!$.

statement: In acute triangle $ABC$, the angle bisector from $A$ meets $BC$ at $L$ and the circumcircle again at $N$. Let $K,M$ be the feet from $L$ to $AB,AC$. Prove quadrilateral $AKNM$ has the same area as $ABC$.
solution:
Set $\angle A=2\alpha$. The equal right triangles $AKL,AML$ give $KM\perp AN$. Also $AK=AL\cos\alpha$, so
$$KM=2AK\sin\alpha=AL\sin2\alpha.$$
Thus the quadrilateral has area $AN\cdot KM/2$.

Triangles $ABL$ and $ANC$ are similar: their angles at $A$ agree, and $\angle ABL=\angle ANC$ by the inscribed-angle theorem. Therefore $AB\cdot AC=AL\cdot AN$. Consequently
$$[ABC]=\tfrac12 AB\cdot AC\sin2\alpha=\tfrac12 AN\cdot AL\sin2\alpha=\tfrac12 AN\cdot KM=[AKNM].$$

statement: If real $x_1,\ldots,x_n$ satisfy $\sum x_i^2=1$, prove that for each integer $k\ge2$ there are integers $a_i$, not all zero, with $|a_i|\le k-1$ and $|\sum a_ix_i|\le (k-1)\sqrt n/(k^n-1)$.
solution:
Consider the $k^n$ sums $\sum b_i|x_i|$ for integer choices $0\le b_i\le k-1$. All lie in $[0,(k-1)\sum|x_i|]$, an interval of length at most $(k-1)\sqrt n$ by Cauchy–Schwarz.

If two sums coincide, subtract their distinct coefficient vectors to obtain a nonzero vector with dot product zero. Otherwise sort all sums increasingly. The $k^n-1$ consecutive gaps have total at most $(k-1)\sqrt n$, so one gap is at most $(k-1)\sqrt n/(k^n-1)$. Subtract the two coefficient vectors giving that gap. Their entries have absolute value at most $k-1$ and are not all zero. Finally reverse the sign of the corresponding coefficient wherever $x_i<0$ to replace $|x_i|$ by $x_i$.
ratingReason: Place all bounded-coefficient linear combinations in an interval, use the smallest adjacent gap, and control the interval length by Cauchy–Schwarz.

statement: Prove no function $f:\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\to\mathbb Z_{\ge0}$ satisfies $f(f(n))=n+1987$ for every $n\ge0$.
solution:
Suppose such an $f$ exists and let $N=\mathbb Z_{\ge0}$. The equation makes $f$ injective: equal values at $m,n$ would imply $m+1987=n+1987$.

Put $A=N\setminus f(N)$. Injectivity implies
$$f(A)=f(N)\setminus f(f(N)).$$
Indeed, the image of a point outside $f(N)$ cannot coincide with the image of a point inside $f(N)$, and every element of the displayed difference has such a preimage.

Consequently the disjoint sets $A,f(A)$ partition $N\setminus f(f(N))=\{0,1,\ldots,1986\}$. They are finite and have equal cardinality because $f$ is injective. Their union must therefore have even cardinality, contradicting its size 1987.

statement: For every integer $n\ge3$, construct $n$ plane points with all pairwise distances irrational and every three forming a nondegenerate triangle of rational area.
solution:
Take $P_j=(j,j^2)$ for $j=1,\ldots,n$. For $j>i$,
$$P_iP_j=(j-i)\sqrt{1+(i+j)^2}.$$
The integer under the square root lies strictly between $(i+j)^2$ and $(i+j+1)^2$, so it is not a square and its square root is irrational. Multiplying by the nonzero integer $j-i$ preserves irrationality.

For $i<j<k$, the determinant area formula gives
$$[P_iP_jP_k]=\frac{(j-i)(k-i)(k-j)}2.$$
This is positive and rational. Thus the construction has both required properties.
ratingReason: Integer points on a parabola simultaneously give nonzero rational determinants and distances involving integers strictly between consecutive squares.

statement: Let $n\ge2$. Suppose $k^2+k+n$ is prime for every integer $0\le k\le\sqrt{n/3}$. Prove it is prime for every integer $0\le k\le n-2$.
solution:
Write $F(k)=n+k(k+1)$ and $r=\lfloor\sqrt{n/3}\rfloor$. Induct from the assumed range. Suppose $r<b\le n-2$ and all earlier $F(i)$ are prime. Since $n<3b^2$, we have $F(b)<(2b+1)^2$.

For $b+1\le j\le2b$, put $i=j-b-1$, so $0\le i<b$. Then $F(b)-F(i)=(b-i)j$. If $F(b)$ and $j$ shared a prime divisor, it would divide the prime $F(i)$, so $F(i)\mid j$. But $j\le2b\le2n-4<2F(i)$, forcing $j=F(i)$. The equality $b+i+1=n+i(i+1)$ becomes $b+1=n+i^2$, impossible because $b\le n-2$. Thus $F(b)$ is coprime to every integer in $(b,2b]$.

Every integer $d\le b$ has a power-of-two multiple in $(b,2b]$, so $F(b)$ is also coprime to every $d\le b$. It has no divisor between 2 and $2b$, while its square root is below $2b+1$. Hence it is prime. This completes the induction; $n=2$ is already in the assumed range.

statement: For every positive integer $d\notin\{2,5,13\}$, prove some distinct $a,b\in\{2,5,13,d\}$ make $ab-1$ nonsquare.
solution: Suppose $2d-1,5d-1,13d-1$ were all squares. Squares modulo sixteen lie in $\{0,1,4,9\}$. The first condition forces $d\equiv1,5,9,13\pmod{16}$. For $d\equiv1$ or 13, $13d-1$ has residue 12 or 8, impossible for a square. For $d\equiv5$ or 9, $5d-1$ has residue 8 or 12, also impossible. Hence at least one of the three products involving $d$ is nonsquare. Its two factors are distinct by the hypothesis on $d$.

statement: Start from any plane point $P_0$. Repeatedly rotate $120^\circ$ clockwise about $A_1,A_2,A_3,A_1,\ldots$ to obtain $P_1,P_2,\ldots$. If $P_{1986}=P_0$, prove triangle $A_1A_2A_3$ is equilateral.
solution:
Use complex coordinates and put $\omega=e^{-2\pi i/3}$. Rotation about $a$ sends $z$ to $\omega z+(1-\omega)a$. Composing the three rotations sends
$$z\longmapsto z+t,\qquad t=(1-\omega)(\omega^2a_1+\omega a_2+a_3),$$
because $\omega^3=1$. After 1986 steps there have been 662 identical blocks, so $P_{1986}=P_0$ forces $662t=0$, hence $t=0$.

Using $1+\omega+\omega^2=0$, this becomes
$$a_3-a_1=-\omega(a_2-a_1).$$
The multiplier $-\omega$ has modulus one and angle $60^\circ$. Thus $A_1A_3=A_1A_2$ and their included angle is $60^\circ$, so all three sides are equal.
ratingReason: Compose one block of three rotations as a translation; returning after 662 blocks forces that translation to vanish, and its complex coefficient identifies an equilateral triangle.

statement: Integers on a pentagon have positive total. Whenever three consecutive labels are $x,y,z$ with $y<0$, one may replace them by $x+y,-y,z+y$. Must repeated legal moves always stop?
solution:
Yes. Let the cyclic labels be $a_1,\ldots,a_5$ and their total be $S>0$, which the operation preserves. Define the nonnegative integer
$$V=\sum_{i=1}^5a_i^2+\sum_{i=1}^5(a_i+a_{i+1})^2,$$
with cyclic indices. Suppose the operated negative label is $a_1=a$, with neighbours $a_5=e,a_2=b$, and remaining labels $c,d$.

The change in the first sum is $2a(a+b+e)$. The adjacent pair sums change from $a+b,b+c,c+d,d+e,e+a$ to $b,a+b+c,c+d,d+e+a,e$, so their squared-sum change is $2a(c+d)$. Therefore
$$V_{\rm new}-V=2aS<0.$$
A nonnegative integer cannot decrease strictly infinitely often. Thus every sequence of legal moves terminates, necessarily with all labels nonnegative.
ratingReason: The invariant positive total makes a quadratic expression decrease at every legal move; discovering the combination of single-entry and adjacent-pair squares supplies termination for every move order.

statement: Let $A,B$ be adjacent vertices of a regular $n$-gon with centre $O$, where $n\ge5$. A rigid triangle $XYZ$, initially $OAB$, moves continuously with $Y,Z$ on the polygon boundary, each traversing that boundary, and $X$ inside. Determine the locus of $X$.
solution:
Let the polygon side be $s$, circumradius $R$, and $\alpha=\pi/n$. The locus is the union of $n$ radial segments beginning at $O$, each directed away from a polygon vertex, of length $R(\sec\alpha-1)$.

Scale $s$ to two. Two boundary points at distance two can lie on the same side only as its endpoints; otherwise they are on adjacent sides. For nonadjacent sides, take their shorter boundary chain and project onto its central direction: that of the middle intervening side, or halfway between the two middle directions. The end segments and all intervening sides have nonnegative projection. A single middle side contributes two; two middle sides contribute $4\cos\alpha>2$. Equality can occur only at the nearest endpoints of sides separated by one side. Thus no other nonadjacent positions have distance two.

During a transition about a vertex $V$, choose coordinates with $V=(0,0)$ and its inward bisector the positive vertical axis. Write
$$Y=p(-\cos\alpha,\sin\alpha),\quad Z=q(\cos\alpha,\sin\alpha),\quad0\le p,q\le2.$$
The fixed-base constraint is
$$4=(p+q)^2\cos^2\alpha+(p-q)^2\sin^2\alpha.$$
The inward apex of the congruent triangle is $X=(0,(p+q)/(2\sin\alpha))$. Along the continuous transition, $p+q$ runs from 2 to $2\sec\alpha$ and back to 2. Since $O=(0,\csc\alpha)$, this traces exactly the claimed segment. Its far endpoint remains inside the polygon because $\sec\alpha-1<\cos\alpha$ for $\alpha\le\pi/5$, placing the segment within the incircle. The other vertices give the rotated segments. Restoring scale gives the displayed length.
ratingReason: Analyse one transition around a vertex using the adjacent-side parameters; the rigid triangle’s apex stays on the angle bisector, and a quadratic constraint gives the exact excursion beyond the centre.

statement: Find all $f:[0,\infty)\to[0,\infty)$ satisfying $f(xf(y))f(y)=f(x+y)$, $f(2)=0$, and $f(t)>0$ for $0\le t<2$.
solution:
Putting $y=2$ shows $f(x+2)=0$ for all $x\ge0$. Thus the zero set is exactly $[2,\infty)$.

Fix $0\le y<2$, so $f(y)>0$. For every $x\ge0$, the equation implies
$$x\ge2-y\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad f(x+y)=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad xf(y)\ge2.$$
The two closed half-line thresholds must agree, giving $f(y)=2/(2-y)$.

Therefore the only candidate is $f(t)=2/(2-t)$ for $t<2$, and zero for $t\ge2$. If $y\ge2$, both sides of the equation vanish. If $y<2$ and $x+y\ge2$, both vanish again. Otherwise direct substitution gives
$$f(xf(y))f(y)=\frac{2-y}{2-y-x}\frac2{2-y}=\frac2{2-x-y}=f(x+y).$$
Hence this candidate works and is unique.
ratingReason: Use the functional equation to identify the full zero set; comparing the zero thresholds in x on both sides determines every positive value without assuming continuity.

statement: Given finitely many integer-coordinate points in the plane, can they always be coloured red and white so that every horizontal or vertical line has colour counts differing by at most one?
solution:
Yes. In each horizontal line, pair its points arbitrarily, leaving at most one unpaired. Do the same independently in each vertical line. Form a graph whose vertices are the given points and whose edges are these pairs.

Each vertex has at most one horizontal edge and at most one vertical edge, so every component is a path, an isolated vertex, or a cycle. On a cycle the edge types alternate, so the cycle has even length. Therefore every component can be coloured alternately red and white, making the endpoints of every pair different colours.

On any horizontal line all its paired points cancel in the colour difference, leaving at most its one unpaired point. The same holds on every vertical line. Hence all required differences are at most one.
ratingReason: Pair points separately in every row and column; the union of the two matchings consists of paths and even cycles, so alternating colours balance every pair.

statement: A circle has centre on side $AB$ of cyclic quadrilateral $ABCD$ and touches each of $BC,CD,DA$. Prove $AD+BC=AB$.
solution:
Let the circle have centre $O$, radius $r$, and contacts $L\in AD$, $M\in CD$, $N\in BC$. Write $\angle A=\alpha$ and $\angle B=\beta$. The right triangles at the tangencies give $AL=r\cot\alpha$, $BN=r\cot\beta$, $AO=r\csc\alpha$, and $BO=r\csc\beta$.

Cyclicity gives $\angle C=\pi-\alpha$ and $\angle D=\pi-\beta$. Since a circle's centre lies on the angle bisector between its two tangents, the other tangent lengths are
$$CN=CM=r\cot(\angle C/2)=r\tan(\alpha/2),$$
$$DL=DM=r\tan(\beta/2).$$
Using $\cot t+\tan(t/2)=\csc t$, we obtain
$$AD+BC=(AL+LD)+(BN+NC)=r(\csc\alpha+\csc\beta)=AO+OB=AB.$$
ratingReason: Express the tangent lengths and centre distances using the angles at the endpoints of the diameter-side; cyclicity supplies supplementary angles and a half-angle identity completes the length equality.

statement: Let $1\le k<n$ with $\gcd(k,n)=1$. Colour $1,\ldots,n-1$ with two colours so that $i,n-i$ always agree and, for $i\ne k$, $i,|i-k|$ agree. Prove all numbers have the same colour.
solution:
Let $r_j$ be the least positive residue of $jk$ modulo $n$, for $1\le j\le n-1$. Coprimality makes these a permutation of $1,\ldots,n-1$.

For $1\le j\le n-2$, put $r=r_j,s=r_{j+1}$. If $s=r+k<n$, then $s$ and $s-k=r$ have the same colour. If $s=r+k-n$, then $n-r=k-s>0$. The first rule equates the colours of $r$ and $n-r$; the second equates those of $s$ and $k-s=n-r$. Thus consecutive residues $r_j,r_{j+1}$ always agree. The entire permutation, and hence every number, has one colour.
ratingReason: The two colour invariances combine into invariance under adding k modulo n; coprimality makes the nonzero multiples of k visit every required residue.

statement: Let $w(P)$ count the odd coefficients of an integer polynomial $P$, and put $Q_i=(1+x)^i$. For $0\le i_1<\cdots<i_n$, prove $w(Q_{i_1}+\cdots+Q_{i_n})\ge w(Q_{i_1})$.
solution:
Reduce coefficients modulo two, so $w$ counts nonzero coefficients. For a power of two $h$, repeated squaring gives $(1+x)^h=1+x^h$. Induct on the largest exponent, with exponent zero immediate.

Let $h$ be its largest power-of-two place. If $i_1\ge h$, factor the sum as $(1+x)^hB$ with $\deg B<h$. Its coefficient blocks are $B$ and $x^hB$, so its weight is $2w(B)$. The induction hypothesis gives $w(B)\ge w((1+x)^{i_1-h})$, and the same disjoint-block identity doubles that last weight to $w(Q_{i_1})$.

If $i_1<h$, split the terms into $A+(1+x)^hB$, where $A$ collects exponents below $h$ and $\deg A,\deg B<h$. The weight is $w(A+B)+w(B)$. Coefficientwise, every nonzero coefficient of $A$ must occur in at least one of $A+B,B$, hence this sum is at least $w(A)$. Induction gives $w(A)\ge w(Q_{i_1})$. Both cases prove the claim.
ratingReason: Work modulo two and split the exponents at their largest binary place; disjoint coefficient blocks double the weight in one case, while the Hamming-weight triangle inequality handles cancellation in the other.

statement: A set contains 1985 distinct positive integers, with no prime divisor greater than 26. Prove that four distinct members have product equal to an integer fourth power.
solution:
Only the nine primes $2,3,5,7,11,13,17,19,23$ can occur. Assign each integer the nine-bit vector of its prime-exponent parities. There are $2^9=512$ vectors, so any 513 available integers contain a pair whose product is a square.

Choose 513 disjoint such pairs successively. This is possible: even after 512 pairs have been removed, $1985-1024=961>512$ integers remain. Write the pair products as $b_1^2,\ldots,b_{513}^2$.

Apply the same parity-vector pigeonhole argument to the 513 integers $b_i$. Two, say $b_i,b_j$, have product $c^2$. The four original integers in those two disjoint pairs then have product $b_i^2b_j^2=c^4$. Their distinctness is guaranteed by the disjoint pairing.
ratingReason: Apply pigeonhole twice to parity vectors of nine prime exponents: first create many disjoint pairs with square products, then pair their square roots to obtain a fourth power.

statement: A circle with centre $O$ meets sides $AB,BC$ of triangle $ABC$ at $A,K$ and $C,N$, respectively, with $K,N$ distinct interior points. The circumcircles of $ABC$ and $KBN$ meet at $B$ and a distinct point $M$. Prove $OM\perp BM$.
solution:
Take $B$ as vector origin, and let unit vectors $u,v$ point toward $A,C$. Write $A=au$, $K=ku$, $C=cv$, $N=nv$. The two circumcircles through the origin have equations
$$|x|^2-l\cdot x=0,\qquad |x|^2-h\cdot x=0,$$
where $l\cdot u=a,l\cdot v=c$ and $h\cdot u=k,h\cdot v=n$.

The circle through $A,K,C,N$ has equation $|x|^2-2o\cdot x+t=0$, where $o$ represents $O$. Restricting to the line in direction $u$ gives a quadratic with roots $a,k$, so $2o\cdot u=a+k$. Likewise $2o\cdot v=c+n$. Since $u,v$ are linearly independent, $2o=l+h$.

At the second intersection $m$, both circle equations give $l\cdot m=h\cdot m=|m|^2$. Therefore $(o-m)\cdot m=0$. These are the vectors $MO$ and $BM$, so the required perpendicularity follows.
ratingReason: Write the two circles through B as quadratic equations with zero constant term; the centre of the third circle is the average of their linear coefficient vectors, making the desired dot product vanish.

statement: For a real initial value $x_1$, define $x_{n+1}=x_n(x_n+1/n)$. Prove that exactly one initial value produces $0<x_n<x_{n+1}<1$ for every $n\ge1$.
solution:
Let $F_n(t)$ be the $n$th term starting at $t$. Each $F_n$ is a strictly increasing polynomial on $[0,\infty)$ with nonnegative coefficients and $F_n(0)=0$. Define $a_n,b_n$ by $F_n(a_n)=1-1/n$ and $F_n(b_n)=1$; thus $a_1=0,b_1=1$.

The recurrence gives $F_{n+1}(a_n)=1-1/n<1-1/(n+1)$ and $F_{n+1}(b_n)=1+1/n>1$. Hence $a_n<a_{n+1}<b_{n+1}<b_n$. The nested closed intervals have a common point $t$, which lies strictly between every pair of endpoints. Therefore $1-1/n<F_n(t)<1$, giving positivity and $F_{n+1}(t)>F_n(t)$.

For uniqueness, convexity and $F_n(0)=0$ imply
$$1-1/n=F_n(a_n)\le\frac{a_n}{b_n}F_n(b_n)=\frac{a_n}{b_n}.$$
Thus $b_n-a_n\le b_n/n\le1/n$, so their common intersection is a single point. Conversely any initial value satisfying the requested inequalities must have $x_n>1-1/n$, hence belong to every interval. This proves exactly one exists.
ratingReason: Define nested intervals of initial values using increasing polynomial iterates; strict endpoint nesting proves existence, while convexity squeezes their widths to zero and proves uniqueness.

statement: For nonnegative $x,y,z$ with $x+y+z=1$, prove $0\le xy+yz+zx-2xyz\le7/27$.
solution:
Write $F=xy+yz+zx-2xyz$. Since $xyz\le xy$ and $xyz\le xz$, we have $F\ge yz\ge0$.

Expanding and using the sum condition gives
$$4F-1=(1-2x)(1-2y)(1-2z).$$
If one variable exceeds $1/2$, exactly one factor is negative and the others nonnegative, so $F\le1/4<7/27$. Otherwise all three factors are nonnegative and their sum is one. AM–GM bounds their product by $1/27$, yielding $F\le(1+1/27)/4=7/27$. The upper bound is attained at $x=y=z=1/3$, and the lower at $(1,0,0)$ and its permutations.
ratingReason: A cubic product identity centres the expression at one quarter; a sign case is essential before applying AM–GM to the transformed factors.

statement: Find positive integers $a,b$ such that $7\nmid ab(a+b)$ but $7^7\mid (a+b)^7-a^7-b^7$.
solution:
Take $(a,b)=(18,1)$. The identity
$$(a+b)^7-a^7-b^7=7ab(a+b)(a^2+ab+b^2)^2$$
follows by expansion. Here $a^2+ab+b^2=324+18+1=343=7^3$, while $ab(a+b)=18\cdot19=342\equiv-1\pmod7$. Thus the required difference is exactly $7^7\cdot342$, and the first condition also holds.

statement: Fix distinct plane points $O,A$. For $X\ne O$, let $\alpha(X)\in[0,2\pi)$ be the counterclockwise angle from $OA$ to $OX$, and let $C(X)$ have centre $O$ and radius $OX+\alpha(X)/OX$. Prove that every finite colouring of the plane has a point $Y$ with $\alpha(Y)>0$ whose colour occurs on $C(Y)$.
solution:
Suppose there are $k$ colours. For each radius $r\in[1,2]$, record the nonempty set of colours appearing on the circle centred at $O$ of radius $r$. There are at most $2^k$ such sets, so among $2^k+1$ distinct radii two, say $r<R$, have the same colour set.

Choose $Y$ at radius $r$ and angle $\theta=r(R-r)$. This angle is strictly positive and less than two, hence less than $2\pi$. By definition, $C(Y)$ has radius $r+\theta/r=R$. The colour of $Y$ appears on the smaller circle and therefore on the larger circle because their colour sets are identical. This is exactly the desired conclusion.
ratingReason: Apply pigeonhole to the finite sets of colours appearing on concentric circles, then tune an angle so that a point on the smaller circle generates the larger one.

statement: A convex quadrilateral $ABCD$ has line $CD$ tangent to the circle with diameter $AB$. Prove that line $AB$ is tangent to the circle with diameter $CD$ exactly when $BC\parallel AD$.
solution:
If $AB\parallel CD$, their distance equals $AB/2$ by the given tangency. The reverse tangency holds exactly when $CD=AB$, which for this convex quadrilateral is exactly the parallelogram condition $BC\parallel AD$.

Otherwise let the supporting lines meet at $O$. Convexity puts each segment on one ray from $O$; reversing the vertex labels if necessary, their orders are $O,A,B$ and $O,D,C$. Let $\theta$ be the angle between the rays. The given tangency says that the distance of the midpoint of $AB$ to line $CD$ equals $AB/2$, namely
$$\sin\theta=\frac{OB-OA}{OB+OA}.$$
The reverse tangency is equivalent to
$$\sin\theta=\frac{OC-OD}{OC+OD}.$$
These two equations are equivalent to $OA/OB=OD/OC$. By the intercept theorem this is equivalent to $AD\parallel BC$.
ratingReason: Express tangency as the ratio of half-chord length to midpoint distance from the intersection of the supporting lines; equality of the two ratios is exactly the intercept theorem.

statement: A convex $n$-gon, $n>3$, has perimeter $p$ and total diagonal length $d$. Prove $n-3<2d/p<\lfloor n/2\rfloor\lfloor(n+1)/2\rfloor-2$.
solution:
Number vertices cyclically. For each diagonal $A_iA_j$, the shifted diagonal $A_{i+1}A_{j+1}$ crosses it. Splitting at their intersection and applying triangle inequalities gives
$$|A_iA_j|+|A_{i+1}A_{j+1}|>|A_iA_{i+1}|+|A_jA_{j+1}|.$$
Sum over all oriented diagonals. Each diagonal length appears four times and each side $2(n-3)$ times, so $4d>2(n-3)p$.

For the upper bound, the sum over $i$ of chords $|A_iA_{i+r}|$ is strictly less than $rp$, by comparing each chord with its $r$-side boundary arc.

If $n=2m+1$, taking $r=2,\ldots,m$ counts every diagonal once. Hence $d<\sum_{r=2}^m rp=[m(m+1)/2-1]p$.

If $n=2m$, take $r=2,\ldots,m-1$ for the nonopposite diagonals. Each of the $m$ opposite-vertex diagonals is shorter than either half-boundary arc and therefore shorter than $p/2$. Thus $d<[\sum_{r=2}^{m-1}r+m/2]p=(m^2/2-1)p$. These are exactly the stated upper bounds.
ratingReason: The lower bound comes from summing strict triangle inequalities for crossing diagonals; the upper bound requires counting boundary arcs separately for odd and even vertex counts.

statement: Odd integers satisfy $0<a<b<c<d$, $ad=bc$, $a+d=2^k$, and $b+c=2^m$. Prove $a=1$.
solution:
Since $d=bc/a$,
$$a+d-b-c=\frac{(b-a)(c-a)}a>0,$$
so $k>m$. Substituting the sums into $ad=bc$ yields
$$(b-a)(b+a)=2^m(b-2^{k-m}a).$$
The parenthesis on the right is odd. Of the two even numbers $b-a,b+a$, exactly one is divisible by four, since their difference $2a$ is twice an odd number. Hence one factor is divisible by $2^{m-1}$.

But $0<b-a<b<2^{m-1}$ because $b<c$ and $b+c=2^m$. Therefore $2^{m-1}\mid b+a$. Also $0<b+a<2b<2^m$, forcing $b+a=2^{m-1}$.

Consequently $b=2^{m-1}-a$, $c=2^{m-1}+a$. The product relation becomes $a(2^k-a)=2^{2m-2}-a^2$, so $a2^k=2^{2m-2}$. Since $a$ is positive and odd, $a=1$.
ratingReason: Compare the two power-of-two sums, then use the exact 2-adic behaviour of b−a and b+a to force their sum to be a single power of two and finish by oddness.

statement: Find all functions $f:(0,\infty)\to(0,\infty)$ satisfying $f(xf(y))=yf(x)$ and $\lim_{x\to\infty}f(x)=0$.
solution:
Put $c=f(1)$. Setting $y=1$ gives $f(cx)=f(x)$. If $c>1$, iterating this equality contradicts the limit; if $c<1$, use $f(x/c)=f(x)$ instead. Hence $c=1$.

Setting $x=1$ now gives $f(f(y))=y$. Substituting $f(y)$ for $y$ in the original equation gives $f(xy)=f(x)f(y)$. In particular $f(1/t)=1/f(t)$.

For any $x$, put $k=xf(x)$. The original equation gives $f(k)=k$. If $k>1$, multiplicativity gives $f(k^n)=k^n$, contradicting the limit. If $k<1$, the same contradiction applies to the fixed point $1/k>1$. Therefore $xf(x)=1$ for every $x$. The function $f(x)=1/x$ directly satisfies both conditions and is the unique answer.
ratingReason: The limit first eliminates a scaling period, giving an involution and then multiplicativity; powers of a nonunit fixed point contradict the limit.

statement: Two intersecting circles with distinct radii have centres $O_1,O_2$ and a common point $A$. Their two common tangents touch them at $P_1,P_2$ and $Q_1,Q_2$. If $M_i$ is the midpoint of $P_iQ_i$, prove $\angle O_1AO_2=\angle M_1AM_2$.
solution:
Take $O_1=(0,0)$, $O_2=(d,0)$, radii $r_1,r_2$, and $A=(x,y)$ with $y>0$. The common external tangents have unit normals $(u,\pm\sqrt{1-u^2})$, where $u=(r_1-r_2)/d$. Hence
$$M_1=(r_1u,0),\quad M_2=(d+r_2u,0),\quad x=\frac{d^2+r_1^2-r_2^2}{2d}.$$
Thus $x$ is the midpoint of the two midpoint coordinates. Put $h=M_1M_2/2=[d^2-(r_1-r_2)^2]/(2d)>0$. The angle $\phi=\angle M_1AM_2$ has $\tan(\phi/2)=h/y$.

Subtracting the two circle equations, or using the altitude formula, gives
$$y^2=\frac{((r_1+r_2)^2-d^2)(d^2-(r_1-r_2)^2)}{4d^2}.$$
For $\theta=\angle O_1AO_2$, the cosine rule yields
$$\tan^2(\theta/2)=\frac{d^2-(r_1-r_2)^2}{(r_1+r_2)^2-d^2}=\frac{h^2}{y^2}=\tan^2(\phi/2).$$
Both half-angles lie in $(0,\pi/2)$, so $\theta=\phi$.
ratingReason: Use the common tangent normals to locate both chord midpoints, then compare half-angle formulas in the two triangles; the unequal radii enter only through their difference.

statement: For pairwise coprime positive integers $a,b,c$, prove that $2abc-ab-bc-ca$ is the largest integer not expressible as $xbc+yca+zab$ with nonnegative integers $x,y,z$.
solution:
Set $F=2abc-ab-bc-ca$. If $F=xbc+yca+zab$, reduction modulo $a,b,c$ gives $x\equiv-1\pmod a$, $y\equiv-1\pmod b$, $z\equiv-1\pmod c$. Nonnegativity then implies
$$xbc+yca+zab\ge(a-1)bc+(b-1)ca+(c-1)ab=F+abc>F,$$
a contradiction.

Now take any integer $N>F$. Choose $0\le x<a$, $0\le y<b$, $0\le z<c$ such that $xbc\equiv N\pmod a$, $yca\equiv N\pmod b$, $zab\equiv N\pmod c$. Pairwise coprimality makes these choices possible. For $S=xbc+yca+zab$, the difference $N-S$ is divisible by $abc$. Since $S\le F+abc$ and $N>F$, we have $N-S>-abc$. Thus $N-S=tabc$ for an integer $t\ge0$, and $N=(x+ta)bc+yca+zab$ is represented. The argument also covers parameters equal to one.
ratingReason: Choose three bounded residues independently modulo the pairwise coprime parameters; their combined upper bound leaves a nonnegative multiple of abc, while the proposed exception forces all three residues maximal.

statement: Colour every point on the boundary of an equilateral triangle with one of two colours. Must there be three same-coloured points forming a right triangle?
solution:
Yes. Mark $X,Y,Z$ two-thirds along the directed sides $BC,CA,AB$, respectively. Then $XY\perp BC$, $YZ\perp CA$, and $ZX\perp AB$. Two marked points share a colour; by cyclic relabelling suppose $X,Y$ are red.

If no monochromatic right triangle exists, every point of $BC$ other than $X$ must be blue. Let $W$ be the perpendicular foot of $Z$ on $BC$; it is an interior point distinct from $X$. The points $B,W$ are blue, so $Z$ must be red, or $BWZ$ would be a blue right triangle.

Now $Y,Z$ are red, forcing every point of $CA$ except $Y$ blue. In particular $A,C$ are blue. The midpoint $M$ of $BC$ is also blue, and $AM\perp BC$. Thus $AMC$ is a blue right triangle, a contradiction.
ratingReason: Three specially placed boundary points contain a same-colour pair whose perpendicular line forces almost an entire side to the other colour; repeating this creates a monochromatic altitude triangle.
notes: Official released paper checked. Mathematical statement paraphrased; original worked exposition checked independently, with John Scholes’s worked solution as a comparison source.

statement: Can one select 1983 distinct integers from $1,\ldots,100000$ with no three forming an arithmetic progression? Prove the answer.
solution:
Yes. Consider all integers with at most eleven ternary digits, each digit zero or one. There are $2^{11}=2048$ such integers, ranging from zero to $(3^{11}-1)/2=88573$.

If three members satisfy $x+z=2y$, neither the addition on the left nor the doubling on the right involves carries in base three. Digitwise, $x_i+z_i=2y_i$ with all digits in $\{0,1\}$. If $y_i=0$, both other digits are zero; if $y_i=1$, both are one. Thus $x=y=z$, so no nonconstant three-term progression occurs.

Add one to every member. This preserves the absence of progressions and produces 2048 positive integers at most 88574. Any 1983 of them are a valid selection.
ratingReason: Base-three digits restricted to zero and one prevent carries in the arithmetic-progression equation, giving a large explicit progression-free set.
notes: Official released paper checked. Mathematical statement paraphrased; original worked exposition checked independently, with John Scholes’s worked solution as a comparison source.

statement: For the side lengths $a,b,c$ of a nondegenerate triangle, prove $a^2b(a-b)+b^2c(b-c)+c^2a(c-a)\ge0$ and determine equality.
solution:
Write $a=y+z$, $b=z+x$, $c=x+y$ with $x,y,z>0$. Expanding the target expression gives
$$2\bigl(xy^3+yz^3+zx^3-xyz(x+y+z)\bigr)
=2xyz\left(\frac{y^2}{z}+\frac{z^2}{x}+\frac{x^2}{y}-x-y-z\right).$$
Cauchy–Schwarz gives
$$\frac{y^2}{z}+\frac{z^2}{x}+\frac{x^2}{y}\ge\frac{(x+y+z)^2}{x+y+z}=x+y+z.$$
Equality requires $y/z=z/x=x/y$, forcing $x=y=z$ because they are positive. Thus equality holds exactly when $a=b=c$.
ratingReason: The triangle-side substitution exposes a cyclic reciprocal sum; Cauchy–Schwarz proves it and its equality condition gives the equilateral case.
notes: Official released paper checked. Mathematical statement paraphrased; original worked exposition checked independently, with John Scholes’s worked solution as a comparison source.

statement: A function $f:\mathbb Z_{>0}\to\mathbb Z_{\ge0}$ has $f(m+n)-f(m)-f(n)\in\{0,1\}$, $f(2)=0$, $f(3)>0$, and $f(9999)=3333$. Determine $f(1982)$.
solution:
The condition at $1+1$ gives $f(1)=0$, and then $f(3)=1$. Repeated superadditivity gives $f(3k)\ge k$. If this were strict for any $k\le3333$, adding $3333-k$ further threes would contradict $f(9999)=3333$. Thus $f(3k)=k$ throughout that range.

Now $1982=1980+2$ gives $f(1982)\ge f(1980)=660$. On the other hand,
$$3f(1982)\le f(5946)=1982,$$
so the integer $f(1982)\le660$. Hence it equals $660$. The data are consistent, for example with $f(n)=\lfloor n/3\rfloor$.
ratingReason: Superadditivity forces exact values on multiples of three up to the prescribed endpoint; tripling the requested input then squeezes its value between consecutive integers.
notes: Official released paper checked. Mathematical statement paraphrased; original worked exposition checked independently, with John Scholes’s worked solution as a comparison source.

statement: In a scalene triangle $A_1A_2A_3$, let $M_i$ be the midpoint of the side opposite $A_i$ and $T_i$ its incircle contact. Reflect $T_i$ in the internal angle bisector at $A_i$ to obtain $S_i$. Prove that $M_1S_1,M_2S_2,M_3S_3$ are concurrent.
solution:
Scale the incircle to the unit circle centred at zero, and use complex coordinates $t_1,t_2,t_3$ for its contacts. The intersection of tangents at $t_j,t_k$ is
$$a_i=\frac{2t_jt_k}{t_j+t_k}.$$
Reflection in the angle-bisector line through zero and $a_i$ sends $t_i$ to
$$s_i=\frac{a_i}{\bar a_i}\bar t_i=\frac{t_jt_k}{t_i}.$$
Consequently direct subtraction gives, for each pair $i,j$,
$$s_i-s_j=K(a_i-a_j),\qquad K=\frac{(t_1+t_2)(t_2+t_3)(t_3+t_1)}{2t_1t_2t_3}.$$
Conjugating the expression shows $K$ is real. Thus $s_i=Ka_i+v$ for a fixed $v$.

The midpoint coordinates satisfy $m_i=(a_1+a_2+a_3-a_i)/2$, so $s_i=\lambda m_i+w$ with real $\lambda=-2K$ and fixed $w$. The circumradius of the $S$-triangle is one, while that of the midpoint triangle is $R/2$, where $R$ is the original circumradius. Hence $|\lambda|=2/R<1$, by the strict Euler inequality $R>2r=2$ for a nonequilateral triangle. In particular $\lambda\ne1$.

The fixed point $h=w/(1-\lambda)$ satisfies $s_i-h=\lambda(m_i-h)$, so all three lines pass through $h$. In a scalene triangle $S_i\ne M_i$: equality would put the side midpoint on the incircle, forcing it to be the contact and the two adjacent sides equal. Thus all three lines are well-defined.
ratingReason: Represent the incircle contacts by unit complex numbers to prove the reflected-contact triangle is homothetic to the original; Euler’s radius inequality rules out the exceptional parallel-line case.
notes: Official released paper checked. Mathematical statement paraphrased; original worked exposition checked independently, with John Scholes’s worked solution as a comparison source.

statement: Let $1=x_0\ge x_1\ge x_2\ge\cdots>0$. Prove some partial sum $\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}x_i^2/x_{i+1}$ is at least $3.999$, and construct such a sequence for which every partial sum is below four.
solution:
Since $(x_i-2x_{i+1})^2\ge0$,
$$\frac{x_i^2}{x_{i+1}}\ge4(x_i-x_{i+1}).$$
Summing gives a lower bound $4(1-x_n)$. If the decreasing sequence tends to zero, this bound exceeds $3.999$ for sufficiently large $n$. If its limit is $\ell>0$, every summand is at least $x_i\ge\ell$, so the partial sums diverge and again exceed $3.999$.

For the construction take $x_i=2^{-i}$. The partial sum is $2+1+\cdots+2^{2-n}=4(1-2^{-n})<4$ for every $n$.
ratingReason: A square identity supplies a telescoping lower bound when the sequence tends to zero; a positive limiting value instead forces divergence. A geometric sequence attains the limiting constant.
notes: Official released paper checked. Mathematical statement paraphrased; original worked exposition checked independently, with John Scholes’s worked solution as a comparison source.

statement: If $x^3-3xy^2+y^3=n$ has an integer solution for a positive integer $n$, prove it has at least three. Show that $n=2891$ has none.
solution:
The transformation $T(x,y)=(y-x,-x)$ preserves the cubic form by expansion, and $T^2(x,y)=(-y,x-y)$, $T^3(x,y)=(x,y)$. A fixed point of either nontrivial power must satisfy $x=y=0$, whose cubic value is zero. Thus any solution for positive $n$ lies in an orbit of three distinct solutions.

Modulo nine, if either variable is divisible by three, the form has residue $0,1$ or $-1$. Otherwise choose $s_x,s_y\in\{1,-1\}$ representing $x,y$ modulo three. Then $x^3\equiv s_x$, $y^3\equiv s_y$ and $3xy^2\equiv3s_x\pmod9$. The form is therefore congruent to $s_y-2s_x\in\{-3,-1,1,3\}$. Since $2891\equiv2\pmod9$, no solution exists.
ratingReason: Find an order-three linear transformation preserving the cubic form, then analyse its possible residues modulo nine to rule out the specified value.
notes: Official released paper checked. Mathematical statement paraphrased; original worked exposition checked independently, with John Scholes’s worked solution as a comparison source.

statement: In regular hexagon $ABCDEF$, points $M\in AC$ and $N\in CE$ satisfy $AM/AC=CN/CE=r$, with $0<r<1$. Determine $r$ when $B,M,N$ are collinear.
solution:
Use coordinates $A=(1,0)$, $B=(1/2,\sqrt3/2)$, $C=(-1/2,\sqrt3/2)$ and $E=(-1/2,-\sqrt3/2)$. Then
$$M=(1-3r/2,\sqrt3r/2),\qquad N=(-1/2,\sqrt3(1-2r)/2).$$
The determinant of $M-B$ and $N-B$ equals
$$(1/2-3r/2)(-\sqrt3r)-(\sqrt3(r-1)/2)(-1)=\frac{\sqrt3}{2}(3r^2-1).$$
It vanishes exactly when $r=\pm1/\sqrt3$. The required interior value is $r=1/\sqrt3$, and substituting it verifies collinearity.
ratingReason: Affine coordinates turn both equal division ratios into linear point formulas; a determinant for collinearity reduces to a single quadratic.
notes: Official released paper checked. Mathematical statement paraphrased; original worked exposition checked independently, with John Scholes’s worked solution as a comparison source.

statement: A simple polygonal path with distinct endpoints lies inside a square of side 100. Every boundary point of the square is within $1/2$ of the path. Prove that two path points at Euclidean distance at most one are separated along the path by length at least 198.
solution:
Parametrise the path in traversal order. Let $A$ be the first square corner whose closed radius-$1/2$ disk the path reaches. Of its neighbouring corners, label the one reached first $B$ and the other $D$. Let $Z$ be the first path point within $1/2$ of $B$, and split the path at $Z$ into an initial and a final part.

On side $AD$, choose the last point $U$ toward $D$ that is within $1/2$ of the initial part. It exists because this covered set is compact and contains $A$; it is not $D$. Every point just beyond $U$ is therefore covered by the final part. Compactness of that part implies that $U$ also lies within $1/2$ of it.

Choose $X$ on the initial part and $Y$ on the final part with $UX,UY\le1/2$. Then $XY\le1$. Also $UB\ge100$ and $BZ\le1/2$, so $XZ\ge99$ and $YZ\ge99$. The subpath from $X$ to $Y$ passes through $Z$ and has length at least $XZ+ZY\ge198$.
ratingReason: Split the path at its first approach to an adjacent corner. A last-covered-point argument on the opposite side, using compactness, produces two nearby points separated by a long excursion.
notes: Official released paper checked. Mathematical statement paraphrased; original worked exposition checked independently, with John Scholes’s worked solution as a comparison source.

statement: For an interior point $P$ of triangle $ABC$, let $D,E,F$ be its perpendicular feet on $BC,CA,AB$. Determine all $P$ minimising $BC/PD+CA/PE+AB/PF$.
solution:
Write $a=BC,b=CA,c=AB$ and $x=PD,y=PE,z=PF$. If the triangle's area is $\Delta$, then $ax+by+cz=2\Delta$. Cauchy–Schwarz gives
$$\left(\frac ax+\frac by+\frac cz\right)(ax+by+cz)\ge(a+b+c)^2.$$
Equality holds exactly when $x=y=z$. The unique interior point equidistant from all three sidelines is the incenter. Thus it uniquely minimises the expression, whose minimum is $(a+b+c)^2/(2\Delta)$.
ratingReason: The area decomposition fixes a weighted sum of the perpendicular distances, and one standard Cauchy–Schwarz application identifies the incenter as the unique equality case.

statement: For $1\le r\le n$, take every $r$-element subset of $\{1,\ldots,n\}$. Show that the average of their minimum elements is $(n+1)/(r+1)$.
solution:
The sum of all minima counts pairs $(S,t)$ where $S$ is an $r$-element subset of $\{1,\ldots,n\}$ and $1\le t\le\min S$. Map this pair to the $(r+1)$-element subset
$$\{t\}\cup\{s+1:s\in S\}\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n+1\}.$$
Its least member is $t$, so the map is bijective: remove the least member and subtract one from all others. Thus the sum of minima is $\binom{n+1}{r+1}$. Dividing by the number $\binom nr$ of subsets gives the stated average.
ratingReason: Count pairs consisting of a subset and an integer below its minimum by adjoining that integer after shifting the subset; the bijection yields the average directly.
notes: Official released paper checked. Mathematical statement paraphrased; original worked exposition checked independently, with John Scholes’s worked solution as a comparison source.

statement: For integers $1\le m,n\le1981$ satisfying $(n^2-mn-m^2)^2=1$, find the maximum of $m^3+n^3$.
solution:
If $n\le m$, then $n^2-mn-m^2\le-m^2$, so the only possibility is $(m,n)=(1,1)$. Otherwise $n>m$. If $m>1$, the relation forces $n<2m$, since $n\ge2m$ would give $n^2-mn-m^2\ge m^2>1$.

The pair $(n-m,m)$ is therefore positive and smaller, and
$$m^2-m(n-m)-(n-m)^2=-(n^2-mn-m^2).$$
Descent ends with $m=1$, where $n=1$ or $2$. Reversing the step gives exactly the consecutive Fibonacci pairs, beginning $(1,1),(1,2),(2,3),(3,5),\ldots$.

The last pair within the bound is $(987,1597)$; the next is $(1597,2584)$. Both coordinates increase along this list, so the maximum is $987^3+1597^3$.
ratingReason: A descent replacing a solution pair by consecutive differences proves that all positive solutions are consecutive Fibonacci numbers; the size bound then fixes the maximal pair.
notes: Official released paper checked. Mathematical statement paraphrased; original worked exposition checked independently, with John Scholes’s worked solution as a comparison source.

statement: For which integers $n>2$ does an interval of $n$ consecutive positive integers have its largest member dividing the least common multiple of the others? For which $n$ is there exactly one such interval?
solution:
Let the largest member be $N\ge n$, and put $L=\operatorname{lcm}(1,\ldots,n-1)$. A prime power $p^e\mid N$ occurs in one of $N-1,\ldots,N-n+1$ exactly when $p^e\le n-1$: subtracting a multiple of $p^e$ from $N$ is necessary, and $N-p^e$ supplies one when the bound holds. Thus the interval works exactly when $N\mid L$ and $N\ge n$.

For $n=3$, $L=2$, so none works. For $n=4$, $L=6$, whose only divisor at least four is six; the unique interval is $3,4,5,6$.

For every $n\ge5$, consecutive integers $n-2,n-1$ are coprime, so $L\ge(n-2)(n-1)\ge2n$. Both $L$ and $L/2$ are distinct divisors of $L$ at least $n$, giving two intervals. Therefore existence holds exactly for $n\ge4$, and uniqueness exactly for $n=4$.
ratingReason: Characterise the admissible largest term through its prime powers, reducing both existence and uniqueness to divisors of lcm(1,...,n−1).
notes: Official released paper checked. Mathematical statement paraphrased; original worked exposition checked independently, with John Scholes’s worked solution as a comparison source.

statement: Three distinct congruent circles lie inside a triangle, each touching a different pair of sides, and have a common point $O$. Prove that $O$, the triangle’s incenter, and its circumcenter are collinear.
solution:
Let $I$ be the incenter, $r$ the inradius, and $\rho$ the common circle radius. Let $D,E,F$ be the centres for the side pairs meeting at $A,B,C$. These centres lie on the respective angle bisectors. Because their distances to their two sides are $\rho$, whereas those of $I$ are $r$, we have
$$D=I+t(A-I),\quad E=I+t(B-I),\quad F=I+t(C-I),\qquad t=1-\rho/r.$$
The circles are distinct, so $\rho<r$ and $t>0$. Thus homothety about $I$ with ratio $t$ maps $ABC$ to $DEF$. If $C_0$ is the original circumcenter, the circumcenter of $DEF$ is $I+t(C_0-I)$. But $OD=OE=OF=\rho$, making $O$ precisely that circumcenter. Hence $O,I,C_0$ are collinear.
ratingReason: Equal distances from the sides make the three circle centres a homothetic copy of the original triangle about its incenter; the common point is the smaller triangle’s circumcenter.
notes: Official released paper checked. Mathematical statement paraphrased; original worked exposition checked independently, with John Scholes’s worked solution as a comparison source.

statement: For nonnegative integers $x,y$, suppose $f(0,y)=y+1$, $f(x+1,0)=f(x,1)$, and $f(x+1,y+1)=f(x,f(x+1,y))$. Determine $f(4,1981)$.
solution:
Induction along successive rows gives
$$f(1,y)=y+2,\qquad f(2,y)=2y+3.$$
Then $f(3,0)=5$ and $f(3,y+1)=2f(3,y)+3$, so $f(3,y)=2^{y+3}-3$.

Put $T_y=f(4,y)+3$. Since $f(4,0)=f(3,1)=13$, we have $T_0=16=2^{2^2}$. The defining recurrence gives $T_{y+1}=2^{T_y}$. Therefore $T_y$ is a right-associated tower of $y+3$ twos. The answer is a tower of $1984$ twos, minus three. These row inductions also show that the recurrence determines the value uniquely.
ratingReason: Resolve the nested recurrence one row at a time, shifting by three in the third and fourth rows to expose repeated doubling and then a power tower.
notes: Official released paper checked. Mathematical statement paraphrased; original worked exposition checked independently, with John Scholes’s worked solution as a comparison source.

statement: Positive integers $p,q$ satisfy $p/q=\sum_{j=1}^{1319}(-1)^{j+1}/j$. Prove $1979\mid p$.
solution:
Subtracting twice the even-indexed terms from the full harmonic sum gives
$$\frac pq=\sum_{j=1}^{1319}\frac1j-\sum_{j=1}^{659}\frac1j=\sum_{j=660}^{1319}\frac1j.$$
Pair $j$ with $1979-j$. Each pair equals $1979/[j(1979-j)]$. The integer 1979 is prime (trial division by primes up to $\sqrt{1979}<45$ suffices), and every denominator factor is less than 1979. Thus the sum is $1979u/v$ for integers $u,v$ with $1979\nmid v$. From $pv=1979uq$, primality gives $1979\mid p$.
ratingReason: Rewrite the alternating harmonic sum as a consecutive tail, then pair denominators summing to 1979; primality ensures the numerator factor survives cancellation.
notes: Official released paper checked. Mathematical statement paraphrased; original worked exposition checked independently, with John Scholes’s worked solution as a comparison source.

statement: Two pentagons have vertices $A_1,\ldots,A_5$ and $B_1,\ldots,B_5$. Colour their ten sides and every segment $A_iB_j$ red or green. If no triangle whose three sides are coloured is monochromatic, prove the ten pentagon sides share one colour.
solution:
If two sides at $A_1$ had different colours, choose three $B$-vertices joined to $A_1$ in one colour, say red, and let $A_1A_2$ be red. All three joins from $A_2$ must be green. Among three vertices of a pentagon two are adjacent. Their connecting side would form a monochromatic triangle with either $A_1$ or $A_2$, regardless of its colour. Thus the $A$-pentagon is monochromatic; the same argument applies to $B$.

Suppose their colours differ, say the $A$ sides are red and the $B$ sides green. Each $A_i$ can have at most two green joins to $B$, because three would include adjacent $B$-vertices and give a green triangle. Hence each of $A_1,A_2$ has at least three red joins. Their two three-element neighbour sets intersect, producing a red triangle with side $A_1A_2$. This contradiction proves both pentagons have the same colour.
ratingReason: A three-vertex majority in a pentagon always contains adjacent vertices; applying this twice forces each face monochromatic and then forces their colours to agree.
notes: Official released paper checked. Mathematical statement paraphrased; original worked exposition checked independently, with John Scholes’s worked solution as a comparison source.

statement: Two intersecting circles share $A$. Two points start at $A$ and traverse the respective circles in the same direction, each at constant speed, completing one revolution simultaneously. Prove there is a fixed point equidistant from the moving points at every instant.
solution:
Let the centres be $O_1,O_2$, and reflect $A$ across the perpendicular bisector of $O_1O_2$ to obtain $P$. Denote this reflection by $S$. At any instant the two radius vectors have undergone the same rotation $R_\theta$. Since reflection reverses rotation, $SR_\theta=R_{-\theta}S$.

Write $u=A-O_1$, $v=A-O_2$, and let $L$ be the linear part of $S$. Then $P-O_2=Lu$ and $P-O_1=Lv$. Thus the squared distances from $P$ are $|R_\theta u-Lv|^2$ and $|R_\theta v-Lu|^2$. Their norm terms agree. Their dot-product terms agree too, since $LR_\theta$ is a reflection and therefore a symmetric linear map:
$$(R_\theta u)\cdot Lv=u\cdot(LR_\theta)v=(R_\theta v)\cdot Lu.$$
Consequently the two distances are equal for every $\theta$.
ratingReason: Reflect the starting point in the perpendicular bisector of the centres; the resulting crossed radii and reflection-reversed angles give congruent triangles throughout the common rotation.
notes: Official released paper checked. Mathematical statement paraphrased; original worked exposition checked independently, with John Scholes’s worked solution as a comparison source.

statement: Let $P$ lie in a plane and $Q$ lie outside it. Determine all points $R$ of the plane maximising $(QP+PR)/QR$.
solution:
Let $X$ be the perpendicular foot of $Q$, and put $d=PX$, $h=QX$, $a=PQ=\sqrt{d^2+h^2}$. For fixed $x=PR$, the denominator is smallest when $R$ lies on ray $PX$ if $d>0$. Then $QR=\sqrt{(x-d)^2+h^2}$ and Cauchy–Schwarz gives
$$\frac{a+x}{QR}=\frac{(x-d)+h\,(a+d)/h}{\sqrt{(x-d)^2+h^2}}\le\sqrt{1+\frac{(a+d)^2}{h^2}}.$$
Equality holds exactly when $x-d=h^2/(a+d)=a-d$, hence $PR=a$. Thus if $P\ne X$ there is one maximiser: the point on ray $PX$ at distance $PQ$ from $P$. If $P=X$, the same calculation is independent of direction, and the maximisers form the circle in the plane centred at $P$ with radius $PQ$.
ratingReason: For each fixed distance from P, move toward the perpendicular foot to minimise the denominator; Cauchy–Schwarz then gives the exact maximum and its equality locus.
notes: Official released paper checked. Mathematical statement paraphrased; original worked exposition checked independently, with John Scholes’s worked solution as a comparison source.

statement: Find all real $a$ for which nonnegative reals $x_1,\ldots,x_5$ satisfy $\sum_{k=1}^5kx_k=a$, $\sum_{k=1}^5k^3x_k=a^2$, and $\sum_{k=1}^5k^5x_k=a^3$.
solution:
Multiply the first equation by $a^2$, subtract twice $a$ times the second, and add the third. This gives
$$\sum_{k=1}^5k(k^2-a)^2x_k=0.$$
Every summand is nonnegative. If every $x_k=0$, then $a=0$, which is valid. Otherwise some $x_j>0$, forcing $a=j^2$. Conversely for $a=j^2$, choose $x_j=j$ and all other coordinates zero; all three equations hold. Therefore the full answer is $a\in\{0,1,4,9,16,25\}$.
ratingReason: A weighted sum of the three moment equations becomes a sum of nonnegative squares; its vanishing confines all nonzero coordinates to one index, with zero needing separate attention.

statement: A walk starts at vertex $A$ of a regular octagon and at each step moves to an adjacent vertex, stopping at its first visit to the opposite vertex $E$. If $a_n$ counts walks stopping after exactly $n$ steps, prove $a_{2n-1}=0$ and $a_{2n}=((2+\sqrt2)^{n-1}-(2-\sqrt2)^{n-1})/\sqrt2$.
solution:
Parity of distance to $E$ changes at every step, so odd stopping times are impossible. Put $A_n=a_{2n}$ and let $B_n$ count walks stopping at $E$ after $2n$ steps when starting two edges from $E$. Looking at the first two moves gives, for $n\ge2$,
$$A_n=2A_{n-1}+2B_{n-1},\qquad B_n=A_{n-1}+2B_{n-1}.$$
Here paths reaching $E$ during those first two moves contribute only when $n=1$, and are excluded for $n\ge2$. Initially $A_1=0,B_1=1$, so $A_2=2$. Eliminating $B$ yields $A_n=4A_{n-1}-2A_{n-2}$ for $n\ge3$. The two characteristic roots are $2\pm\sqrt2$; the initial values give
$$A_n=\frac{(2+\sqrt2)^{n-1}-(2-\sqrt2)^{n-1}}{\sqrt2},$$
as required.
ratingReason: Introduce an auxiliary starting vertex to obtain a two-state recurrence, then eliminate it and solve the resulting second-order recurrence with the correct absorbing boundary.

statement: For positive integers $m<n$, the last three decimal digits of $1978^m$ and $1978^n$ coincide. Find the pair minimising $m+n$.
solution: Put $d=n-m$. Divisibility by eight of $1978^m(1978^d-1)$ forces $m\ge3$, since the second factor is odd. Modulo 125, the base is 103. Modulo five its order is four, so $4\mid d$. Directly $103^2\equiv109$ and $103^4\equiv6\pmod{125}$. Writing $d=4t$, the binomial theorem gives $6^t\equiv1+5t+25t(t-1)/2\pmod{125}$. First modulo 25 this forces $5\mid t$. For $t=5s$, the quadratic term vanishes modulo 125 and $6^t\equiv1+25s$, so $5\mid s$. Therefore $100\mid d$, and $d=100$ works. The least pair is $(m,n)=(3,103)$, with sum 106.

statement: Fix a point $P$ inside a sphere of radius $R$ and centre $O$. Three mutually perpendicular rays from $P$ meet the sphere at $U,V,W$. Complete the rectangular box with edges $PU,PV,PW$, and let $Q$ be opposite $P$. Determine the full locus of $Q$.
solution:
The locus is the sphere centred at $O$ with radius $\sqrt{3R^2-2OP^2}$.

Take $O$ as origin, write $p=\overrightarrow{OP}$, and put $c=R^2-|p|^2>0$. Let the three unit directions be $e_i$ and edge lengths $t_i$. The sphere equations give $t_i^2+2t_i(p\cdot e_i)=c$. For $q=p+\sum t_ie_i$, adding gives $|q|^2=|p|^2+3c$.

Conversely take any $q$ with that norm. Define $H(e)=(q\cdot e)^2-(p\cdot e)^2$ on unit vectors. Its values on every orthonormal triple sum to $3c$. Start with any such triple; its minimum and maximum values bracket $c$, so continuity along a spherical path supplies a unit $e_1$ with $H(e_1)=c$. On the perpendicular plane, the values at perpendicular unit vectors sum to $2c$; continuity around its unit circle supplies $e_2$ with value $c$, and its perpendicular $e_3$ then also has value $c$.

Orient each $e_i$ so that $t_i=(q-p)\cdot e_i>0$. This is possible because $H(e_i)=c>0$ rules out $t_i=0$. The equation $H(e_i)=c$ becomes $t_i^2+2t_i(p\cdot e_i)=c$, so $p+t_ie_i$ lies on the original sphere. These rays yield exactly $q$, proving the converse.
ratingReason: A vector identity gives the containing sphere, but proving the entire sphere is attained requires choosing an orthonormal basis on which a quadratic form has equal diagonal values.

statement: Increasing positive-integer sequences $f(1),f(2),\ldots$ and $g(1),g(2),\ldots$ partition the positive integers and satisfy $g(n)=f(f(n))+1$. Determine $f(240)$.
solution:
We have $f(1)=1$, since $g(1)\ge2$. No two consecutive integers lie in the $g$ sequence: the predecessor of $g(n)$ is $f(f(n))$.

If $f(n)=k$, count the integers up to $g(n)=f(k)+1$. Exactly $k$ belong to the $f$ sequence and exactly $n$ to the $g$ sequence. Hence $f(k)=n+k-1$. The next integer after $g(n)$ belongs to the $f$ sequence, giving $f(k+1)=n+k+1$.

Starting with $f(1)=1$, these two rules successively give
$$f(2)=3,\ f(3)=4,\ f(4)=6,\ f(6)=9,\ f(9)=14,$$
$$f(14)=22,\ f(22)=35,\ f(35)=56,\ f(56)=90,$$
$$f(91)=147,\ f(148)=239,\ f(240)=388.$$
Thus the required value is $388$.
ratingReason: Complementarity yields two self-indexing recursion rules; use a carefully chosen chain of known values to reach the requested index.
